sentences.text: The genus Herbstosaurus contains only one known species, H. pigmaeus, which is known from a partial skeleton.
The dispersed bones of the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — are compressed and crushed by the weight of the overlying rock layers.
Herbstosaurus has generated special interest because it is likely one of the oldest known pterodactyloids.
The reclassification of Herbstosaurus as a pterosaur allowed some fragmentary pterosaur material from the same layers, including a wing bone, to be referred to the genus.
Argentine paleobotanist Rafael Herbst discovered disarticulated bones of a small reptile in a sandstone nodule at Picun Leufú in Neuquén Province in 1969.
Paleontologist Rodolfo Magín Casamiquela named the fossil as the new species Herbstosaurus pigmaeus in 1975.
The genus name honors Rafael Herbst and connects it to the Greek word for lizard, and Casamiquela originally assumed it was a small theropod dinosaur.
The species name derives from the Greek for dwarf, as it was thought to represent a small Compsognathus-like theropod and one of the smallest dinosaurs known at the time.
Casamiquela noted that the species was distinct due to an atypically long ilium and short ischium.
In 1978, John Ostrom concluded that the long ilium and short ischium indicated Herbstosaurus was a pterosaur rather than a dinosaur.
In 2025, Ezcurra et al. reanalyzed the holotype and scored it in a phylogenetic dataset to determine its relationships with other pterosaurs.
It was later determined that Herbstosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic (Tithonian) based on its discovery in the Vaca Muerta Formation.
Herbstosaurus lived during the Tithonian stage, approximately 149.2 to 143.1 million years ago.
Peter Wellnhofer suggested in 1991 that Herbstosaurus was a more basal pterosaur rather than a pterodactyloid due to the form of its pelvis.
The conclusion that Herbstosaurus was a basal pterosaur was doubted by Laura Codorniú and Zulma Gasparini in 2007.
